summary: A note from BBN after an IMP software update added a delay of about 30 seconds before the IMP accepted messages from a host that had just come up. Some host programs had timeouts that treated this as a failure and shut down. BBN asked that BBN Report 1822 be treated as the fixed, authoritative description of the host-IMP interface.

plainLanguage.summary: A shop changed how long its door takes to open, and some customers decided the shop was closed and left. The shop says sorry and asks everyone to follow the written rules for the door.

questions: why did ncp shut down after imp update
subtitle: A memo clarifying the host-IMP interface after a software update caused confusion

tldr.problem: BBN updated the IMP software to fix a bug, adding a 30-second delay before accepting messages from hosts that just came up. Some host programs had shorter timeout limits and treated this delay as a failure, causing them to shut down.
tldr.mechanism: BBN requested that all hosts treat BBN Report 1822 as the definitive and invariant specification of the host-IMP interface, and not rely on undocumented behavior or experimental extrapolation.
tldr.outcome: This established the principle that the host-IMP interface should be strictly documented and understood by all participants, with BBN working on an updated 1822 report.

today: This note helped establish the principle that network interfaces must be precisely documented and adhered to, a foundational concept in protocol design still followed today.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
On 25 June 1971, BBN deployed IMP system version 2500 with a correction to prevent hosts from receiving spurious "Destination Dead" messages. The fix added a constraint: the IMP would refuse to accept any messages from a host for about 30 seconds after the host indicated it was coming alive.

This delay caused trouble for host programs using the Network Control Protocol (NCP). Some had imposed upper limits on the acceptable time for an IMP to accept a message. When the new delay exceeded those limits, the programs declared the IMP inoperative and shut themselves down.
sections.plainLanguage: A software fix added a waiting period, and some host programs had stricter rules and thought the system was broken.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
BBN acknowledged causing confusion but argued the change did not modify any advertised property of the system. To prevent such misunderstandings in the future, the IMP/Host interface needed to be well documented, well understood, and invariant.

BBN proposed that the host-IMP interface should be defined and maintained based on BBN Report No. 1822, treated as complete and correct. Hosts should operate under the assumption that anything not specifically guaranteed by 1822 does not exist and should not be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Misunderstandings come from unclear rules. The solution is to follow the written specification exactly.

sections.title: Next Steps
sections.content: BBN committed to working on an update to 1822 to reflect recent changes, such as the deletion of the "cease" mechanism described in RFC 107. The team also planned to augment the IMP/Host protocol with a mechanism allowing hosts to detect changes in the IMP system version and to provide hosts with status information about which systems in the network were alive.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book would be updated to match the actual system, and new ways would be added for computers to check on each other's status.

references.text: RFC 107: "Some host software proposals for the ARPANET and comments on the NWG/RFC 733 proposed mail protocol."
